paper_a.title: On Model Selection Consistency of Lasso

paper_b.title: High-Dimensional Graphs and Variable Selection with the Lasso

metadata.description: Both papers (published essentially in parallel in 2006) establish Lasso support-recovery consistency under an irrepresentable-type condition, but from substantially different angles. Zhao-Yu treat a single sparse linear regression and isolate the Strong/Weak Irrepresentable Condition on the Gram matrix as the (almost) sufficient and necessary requirement for sign consistency, including a fixed-p classical regime and high-dimensional moment/Gaussian regimes. Meinshausen-Buhlmann attack covariance selection in Gaussian graphical models by running per-node Lasso (neighborhood selection); their Assumption 6 (Neighborhood Stability via the signed quantity S_a(b)) is the same population irrepresentable-type condition rephrased through best-linear-prediction coefficients, and they obtain analogous exponential-rate type-I/type-II/edge-set consistency. The relationship is best classified as competing frameworks (CF) on the same underlying support-recovery problem rather than direct rediscovery, since the two papers solve different statistical problems with parallel theory and the M-B paper additionally addresses graph-level aggregation and an oracle-prediction inconsistency that have no Zhao-Yu counterpart.

matches.explanation: Both define the Lasso as L1-penalized least squares. Zhao-Yu state it as the global problem ProbP109.1 = argmin ||Y - X beta||^2 + lambda ||beta||_1; Meinshausen-Buhlmann state it node-wise as the neighborhood Lasso DP110.5 = argmin n^{-1}||X_a - X theta||^2 + lambda ||theta||_1 with theta_a = 0. These are the same estimator applied in two settings (single regression vs per-node regression). Confidence high despite paper109's PDF-fallback because the name 'Lasso Estimator' and the L1+squared-loss form are unambiguous.

Zhao-Yu's DP109.1 is the standard sparse linear-regression model Y = X beta + noise with q nonzero coefficients. Meinshausen-Buhlmann do not assume a regression model directly; instead they assume a Gaussian X with conditional independence graph (DP110.1) and consider the population best-linear-prediction coefficients theta^a (DP110.3) for each node a from the others. The two are analogous: theta^a plays the role of beta in a node-wise regression of X_a on the rest, with the support of theta^a being the neighborhood of a (the analog of the active set in Zhao-Yu). Sparsity assumption is captured separately (see AssumP110.3).

This is the central conceptual identity of the pair. Zhao-Yu's Strong Irrepresentable Condition |C_{21} C_{11}^{-1} sign(beta_{(1)})| <= 1 - eta is exactly Meinshausen-Buhlmann's Neighborhood Stability assumption |S_a(b)| < delta < 1, where S_a(b) = sum_{k in ne_a} sign(theta^{a,ne_a}_k) theta^{b,ne_a}_k (DP110.7). Both quantities measure the signed regression of an irrelevant covariate on the relevant ones using the in-support sign pattern; Zhao-Yu phrase it on the empirical Gram matrix, M-B phrase it on the population best-linear-prediction coefficients restricted to ne_a. The element-wise margin eta in Zhao-Yu plays the role of the fixed gap 1-delta in M-B.

Zhao-Yu's Weak Irrepresentable Condition (strict inequality with no margin) is the necessary form of the irrepresentable condition that arises in their necessity Theorem 2. M-B's Assumption 6 is a sufficient version (with strict gap delta < 1); the necessity counterpart appears as the failure regime |S_a(b)| > 1 in their Proposition 3. Strictly speaking the Weak IC corresponds to the boundary case |S_a(b)| <= 1 used in M-B's Proposition 2 rather than to Assumption 6 itself; analogous match with medium confidence.

Zhao-Yu introduce the explicit block decomposition of the Gram matrix C = (C_11, C_12; C_21, C_22) corresponding to relevant vs irrelevant covariates. M-B implicitly use the analogous split (active neighborhood ne_a vs its complement) throughout but never name a separate node for it; they manipulate the corresponding population coefficients theta^{a,ne_a} and the off-neighborhood gradients G_b directly. No clean L1 counterpart, so flagged as none.

Sign equality =_s is Zhao-Yu's recovery target (matching signs entry-wise, including zeros to zeros). M-B's recovery target is set equality of the estimated and true neighborhood, plus separately sign agreement on the support (Lemma A.2). They never define a single sign-equality predicate at the node level; they split the criterion into the sub-/super-set events {ne_hat subseteq ne_a} (Theorem 1) and {ne_a subseteq ne_hat} (Theorem 2). No paired definition node, so flagged none.

Zhao-Yu's Strong Sign Consistency (deterministic lambda_n) and General Sign Consistency (some path lambda) target asymptotic recovery of sign(beta). M-B's Problem 'Neighborhood selection' (ProbP110.2) sets up the analogous goal of estimating ne_a from data; their consistency claims are stated directly inside Theorems 1, 2 and Corollary 1 rather than as a separate consistency definition. The grouping is analogous because the two papers handle the goal at different granularities: Zhao-Yu fix vocabulary up front, M-B fold it into the theorem statements.

Both papers bundle a parallel set of regularity assumptions before stating their high-dimensional consistency theorems. Zhao-Yu's AssumP109.1 (fixed-p: C^n -> C positive definite, max row-norm vanishing) corresponds to M-B's AssumP110.1 (p = O(n^gamma)) plus AssumP110.2 (Var(X_a)=1, conditional variance bounded below). AssumP109.2's conditions (5)-(8) -- bounded covariate norms (M_1), lower spectrum on C_11 (M_2), sparsity q_n = O(n^c1) (analog of AssumP110.3, max neighborhood = O(n^kappa)), and minimum signal n^{(1-c2)/2} min |beta_i| >= M_3 (analog of AssumP110.5, |pi_ab| >= delta n^{-(1-xi)/2}) -- are the same package up to graphical-model rephrasings. AssumP110.4 (bounded l_1-norm of restricted coefficients) is a graph-specific control with no clean Zhao-Yu twin.

Identical KKT characterization of Lasso solutions. Both lemmas state: at a solution, the loss-gradient equals -lambda * sign(theta_b) on active coordinates and is bounded by lambda in absolute value on inactive ones. M-B add the strict-inequality uniqueness clause (citing Osborne-Presnell-Turlach 2000) but otherwise the statements are the same. This is the workhorse lemma in both papers' proofs.

Zhao-Yu's Proposition 1 isolates the lower bound P(sign-recovery) >= P(A_n cap B_n), where A_n controls the sign on the support and B_n the shrinkage of the off-support coefficients to zero. M-B do not state this as a separate proposition; the same reduction appears in proof step PSP110.4, which reduces the type-I event to the gradient event E = {max_{k not in cl_a} |G_k(theta_hat^{a,ne_a,lambda})| < lambda}. Both reductions use the KKT lemma and isolate the off-support gradient as the binding constraint.

Zhao-Yu's Theorem 1 treats the classical fixed-p regime under regularity (3)-(4) and the Strong Irrepresentable Condition, giving exponential-rate sign consistency. M-B work exclusively in the high-dimensional regime p = O(n^gamma) with Gaussian X; they have no separate fixed-p statement. The fixed-p result is a Zhao-Yu-specific contribution within this pair.

Necessity of the irrepresentable-type condition. Zhao-Yu's Theorem 2 shows that general sign consistency forces the Weak IC eventually. M-B's Proposition 3 shows that if some |S_a(b)| > 1, the type-I event {ne_hat subseteq ne_a} fails: P(.) -> 0. Both establish that some form of the irrepresentable condition is essentially necessary; modulo the difference between sign consistency vs neighborhood-subset consistency, these are the same negative result.

Main consistency theorems of each paper. Zhao-Yu's Theorem 3 (bounded-2k-moment noise) and Theorem 4 (Gaussian noise) give exponential-rate sign consistency with p_n growing polynomially or exponentially in n. M-B's Theorem 1 (no false inclusions) and Theorem 2 (no false exclusions) together with Corollary 1 (edge-set consistency) give analogous P(ne_hat = ne_a) = 1 - O(exp(-c n^epsilon)) in the high-dimensional Gaussian-graphical-model setting. Same exponential rate, same role for the irrepresentable-type condition; differs in problem formulation (single regression with arbitrary X and i.i.d. noise vs Gaussian X with i.i.d. samples).

Both papers offer concrete sufficient-design conditions guaranteeing the irrepresentable-type assumption. Zhao-Yu enumerate equicorrelated (CP109.1), bounded-correlation (CP109.2), AR(1) power-decay (CP109.3), special degenerate designs (CP109.4), and block-wise (CP109.5). M-B give two parallel structural sufficient conditions: cycle-free graphs (RP110.1) and diagonal dominance of Sigma^{-1} (RP110.2). Spirit and role are identical (concrete classes where the abstract condition holds), but the specific design families differ; analogous, medium confidence.

M-B's Proposition 1 -- the prediction-oracle Lasso penalty is variable-selection inconsistent for a simple two-correlated-variable Gaussian -- is a key cautionary contribution unique to paper110 within this pair. It motivates moving away from cross-validation-style penalties. Zhao-Yu do not address oracle-prediction penalties at all. (The PSP children are kept implicit per v2 compactness but the reasoning is the same.)

M-B's Proposition 2 is a population-Lasso lemma showing that neighborhood stability (existence of eta>0 with ne_a(eta) = ne_a(0)) implies |S_a(b)| <= 1. It is a structural justification for naming the assumption 'stability'. Zhao-Yu have no parallel population-Lasso analysis -- their entire derivation is in finite samples on the empirical Gram matrix. Flagged none.

M-B's disturbed neighborhood ne_a(eta) := support of the population Lasso minimizer at penalty eta is a genuinely M-B-specific construct used to derive Proposition 2 and motivate Assumption 6. Zhao-Yu do not consider a population-level penalized objective.

Restricted optimal coefficients theta^{a,A} (best linear prediction of X_a using only A) are an M-B definition supporting their assumption hierarchy and proof manipulations (e.g. theta^{a,ne_b} appears in Assumption 4, theta^{b,ne_a} in DP110.7). Zhao-Yu work directly with the empirical block (C_11)^{-1} sign(beta_{(1)}) and never define a population restricted regression.

Graph-level aggregation (AND/OR edge sets DP110.8, connectivity components DP110.9), the finite-sample component-protection Theorem 3 (TP110.3) with its data-driven penalty schedule lambda(alpha) (EP110.1) and proof PP110.7, are the graph-specific contributions of paper110. Zhao-Yu's setting is single-regression and has no graph-aggregation analog.

M-B's Proposition 4 (necessity of xi > epsilon for detection) and Lemma A.3 (uniform tail bound on the parallel-noise inner product) belong to the type-II/false-exclusion machinery, which Zhao-Yu also need but handle inside their Theorem 3-4 proofs without a separately named lemma. Recorded as none here because the M-B structure has no isolated counterpart node.

Pair-level problem framing. Zhao-Yu's working problem is sparse linear regression / Lasso. M-B explicitly state two problems: covariance selection (ProbP110.1: estimate the conditional independence graph / zeros of Sigma^{-1}) and neighborhood selection (ProbP110.2: estimate ne_a from data). The link is that M-B *reduce* covariance selection to many parallel Lasso problems (ProbP110.2 is essentially Zhao-Yu's ProbP109.1 with X_a as response and the rest as predictors). Analogous because the umbrella problems differ (single sparse regression vs structure learning), but the underlying computational unit is the same Lasso fit.

Proof of Zhao-Yu's Proposition 1 (KKT-driven decomposition into block events A_n and B_n) and proof of M-B's Theorem 1 (KKT-driven reduction to the gradient event E and Bernstein/Bonferroni control of off-neighborhood gradients) play the same structural role: invoke the KKT lemma, isolate the off-support gradient inequality, then bound a tail. The proofs are not identical (Zhao-Yu go through an explicit reparametrization u = beta_hat - beta and asymptotic-normality tail bounds, M-B route through population conditional expansions of X_b on X_{ne_a} plus Bernstein), but the high-level architecture matches. Below this level, the v2 rule allows the composite L2 entry (PSP109.1-4 and PSP110.4-6 listed below) -- omitted here since the L1 parents already capture the alignment.

Proofs of the high-probability sign-recovery theorems. Zhao-Yu's PP109.2 (Theorem 1 fixed-p) and PP109.4 (Theorems 3 and 4 high-dim) reduce to Proposition 1's lower bound and apply Gaussian / bounded-2k-moment tail bounds on z_i and zeta_i. M-B's PP110.5 (Theorem 2: type-II error) reduces via the gradient event E to Lemma A.2's restricted-Lasso sign consistency. Both proofs are structurally similar two-stage (KKT reduction + tail-bound) arguments; analogous match.

Proofs of necessity. Zhao-Yu's PP109.3 (Theorem 2): contradiction argument, if WIC fails infinitely often a Gaussian limit assigns positive probability to the wrong sign. M-B's PP110.4 (Proposition 3): mirror the Theorem 1 proof but reverse the bound -- since |S_a(b)| > 1, the off-support gradient exceeds lambda with probability tending to 1. Same conceptual move (turning the irrepresentable bound from upper to lower drives the failure event), executed in two different proof languages.

Both papers cite the same external LARS algorithm of Efron, Hastie, (Johnstone,) Tibshirani 2004 for computing the full Lasso path. This is an external-vs-external citation match -- no signal for the pair-level relation_type, but recorded for completeness.

The Lasso neighborhood selection algorithm (per-node Lasso plus AND/OR aggregation) is the central methodological proposal of paper110. Zhao-Yu have no algorithmic counterpart at this level; they study the statistical Lasso estimator without proposing a new algorithm.
Forward-selection MLE baseline (Edwards 2000; Lauritzen 1996) is cited by M-B as a comparison method for graphical model estimation; no analog in Zhao-Yu's regression-only setting.

Zhao-Yu cite Knight-Fu's (2000) estimation consistency result for Lasso (with lambda_n = o(n)). M-B do not cite or use this result directly in their extracted graph (their machinery operates in the support-recovery regime with much larger lambda).
Zhao-Yu's coherence-comparison remark (Donoho et al. 2004 require <1/(4q-1) vs Zhao-Yu's <1/(2q-1)) is paper-specific commentary linking their bound to compressed-sensing literature. No M-B analog.
Zhao-Yu's comparison with hard/soft thresholding of OLS in the small-p regime (and its breakdown for p > n) has no direct analog in M-B.

Proofs of Zhao-Yu's design-specific corollaries CP109.1-5 (equicorrelated, bounded-correlation, AR(1), special small designs, block-wise). Each is a direct linear-algebra calculation on the empirical Gram block C_21 (C_11)^{-1} sign(beta_{(1)}). M-B's parallel design results (cycle-free, diagonal dominance) appear only as remarks (RP110.1, RP110.2) without separate proof nodes, so these proofs have no proof-level counterpart.

M-B define the neighborhood ne_a as the smallest separating set of node a in the conditional independence graph (equivalently the set of nodes b with edge (a,b)). Zhao-Yu's analog is the support {i: beta_i != 0} (size q), but it is not given a separate definition node -- it is bundled into DP109.1 (linear regression model).

M-B's Lemma A.2 establishes sign consistency of the *restricted* (oracle-support) Lasso regression with exponential rate. Zhao-Yu's proofs derive the analogous fact inline (see PSP109.6 / PSP109.7 / PSP109.10-12) but not as a separately named lemma. No L1 counterpart, so flagged none.

Proof of M-B's Proposition 2 (population-Lasso KKT subdifferential argument deriving |S_a(b)| <= 1 from neighborhood stability). Zhao-Yu have no population-Lasso proposition and hence no analogous proof.

Proofs of M-B's Lemmas A.1 and A.2. PP110.8 (KKT lemma) is the standard subdifferential argument; Zhao-Yu state Lemma 1 (LP109.1) without a separate extracted proof node. PP110.9 (restricted-Lasso sign consistency) supports the M-B-specific Lemma A.2 which has no Zhao-Yu counterpart (see preceding entry).
